text: Multitasking gets sold as a productivity superpower, but I've come to see it as mostly a flattering myth. Every time I think I'm juggling my reading, a group chat, and a half-written lab report at once, what I'm actually doing is rapidly switching between them and paying a tax each time. My focus snaps back to the document a second slower, I reread the same sentence twice, and the report that should take an hour somehow eats an entire evening. What convinced me wasn't a study so much as my own grades. The semester I started leaving my phone in another room, my essays got tighter and my problem sets stopped having those careless arithmetic slips that come from doing math while answering texts. It turns out the brain isn't really parallel hardware; it's one narrow spotlight that we keep yanking around and calling efficiency. The people I know who seem to multitask well are usually just good at doing one thing fast and then cleanly moving to the next. So no, I don't think multitasking is a skill worth cultivating. The skill actually worth building is its opposite: the discipline to close the other tabs, sit with a single hard task, and let it have my full attention until it's genuinely done.
